title: GitHub Portfolio Guide: How Junior Developers Build a Profile That Gets Interviews
description: What engineering reviewers actually check on a junior developer's GitHub, and how to structure READMEs, commits, tests and CI so your portfolio earns interviews.
body:
When a recruiter or engineering manager opens your GitHub, they are not going to clone your repository, install dependencies and run it. Most reviewers spend a minute or two scanning, and they decide quickly whether there is enough evidence to move you forward. Your job is to make that evidence obvious within those first two minutes.

This GitHub portfolio guide covers what reviewers actually look at, how to structure a README that answers their questions, and the engineering signals (commits, tests, CI, deployment) that separate a hireable portfolio from a folder of tutorials.

## What a reviewer checks in the first 90 seconds

Based on how hiring teams typically review junior candidates, the scan usually goes like this:

1. **Profile page:** a profile README, pinned repositories, a clear name and a link back to your LinkedIn or portfolio.
2. **Top pinned repository:** the README first, then the folder structure, then a couple of source files.
3. **Signals of care:** tests, a CI badge, sensible commit messages, a license, an `.env.example` instead of committed secrets.
4. **Live demo:** if there is a link, they click it. If it is broken, that is the impression they leave with.

If those steps go well, your resume claims become believable. If they do not, a strong resume can still lose to a weaker one with a better-presented portfolio.

## Choose the right projects to pin

Pin three to six repositories, ordered by relevance to the jobs you want. A strong set for a junior developer usually includes:

- **One substantial full project** with a real use case, ideally used by someone other than you.
- **One project that shows depth** in your target area: a backend service with authentication and background jobs, a data pipeline, a mobile app with offline support, an ML model with an evaluation.
- **One open-source contribution or collaboration** that shows you can work in someone else's codebase.
- Optionally, **a small, polished tool or library** that solves one problem well.

Unpin course projects, cloned tutorials and forks you have not changed. They dilute the signal.

## Anatomy of a README that gets read

Treat each pinned README as a one-page technical pitch. A structure that works:

| Section | What to include |
|---|---|
| Title and one-line summary | What it does and for whom, in one sentence |
| Demo | Live link, test credentials or guest mode, and a screenshot or GIF |
| Features | Three to six bullets of what users can do |
| Tech stack | Languages, frameworks, database, hosting |
| Architecture | A simple diagram (Mermaid or Excalidraw) of components and data flow |
| Key decisions | Two or three choices you made and why, including trade-offs |
| Getting started | Exact commands to run locally, ideally one `docker compose up` |
| Testing | How to run tests and what they cover |
| What I would do next | Known limitations and planned improvements |

The **key decisions** section is the one most juniors skip and the one reviewers value most. A paragraph explaining why you chose PostgreSQL over MongoDB for transactional data, or why you used a queue for email sending, shows engineering judgement that code alone does not.

## Commit history and Git workflow

A repository with a single "initial commit" containing ten thousand lines suggests the code was copied or built without version control. You do not need perfection, but you should show a normal workflow:

- **Small, focused commits** with clear messages. Conventional prefixes such as `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:` and `docs:` help, but clarity matters more than format.
- **Branches and pull requests**, even on solo projects. Open a PR for a feature, describe what changed, and merge it. It shows you know how teams work.
- **Issues** for bugs and planned features. A short backlog shows you think about the project beyond today.

## Tests and continuous integration

Tests are one of the strongest signals of engineering maturity in a junior portfolio, because many candidates skip them.

- Add unit tests for core logic and a few integration tests for important flows, such as an API endpoint that writes to the database.
- Run them automatically with **GitHub Actions** on every push and pull request.
- Add linting and type checking to the same workflow.
- Show the status badge at the top of the README.

You do not need high coverage. A focused suite that tests the parts most likely to break is better than a large suite of trivial assertions.

## Deployment and operations

A working deployment answers the question "can this person ship?" Host your frontend on a platform like Vercel or Netlify and your API on a service such as Render, Fly.io, Railway or a small cloud instance. Then go one step further where it makes sense:

- Use environment variables and commit an `.env.example`, never real secrets.
- Add a health check endpoint and basic logging.
- Write a short deployment section in the README explaining how releases happen.

If you accidentally committed a secret, rotate it immediately; deleting the commit is not enough because the history may already be copied.

## Your profile README

A profile README is the small repository named after your username that renders on your profile page. Keep it short:

- One line on what you build and what roles you are looking for.
- Links to your top two projects with one-line descriptions.
- Your core stack as plain text or a small set of badges.
- Contact links.

Skip long animated banners and dozens of statistics cards. They slow the page and push your projects below the fold. The [GitHub README generator](/github) can produce a clean starting version you then edit.

## A one-week upgrade plan

1. **Day 1:** unpin weak repositories and choose your top three.
2. **Day 2:** rewrite the README of your top project using the table above.
3. **Day 3:** add or fix the live demo and screenshots.
4. **Day 4:** add tests for the core logic.
5. **Day 5:** set up a GitHub Actions workflow for tests and linting.
6. **Day 6:** write the key decisions section and an architecture diagram.
7. **Day 7:** update your profile README and link the portfolio from your resume and LinkedIn.

## Get a second opinion

Run your repositories through InternFlow's free [GitHub tools](/github) for README suggestions and code review feedback, then make sure your resume points reviewers to the right place with the [resume builder](/resume/builder). If you are a student in India preparing for campus or off-campus hiring, our [GitHub portfolio builder guide for Indian students](/blog/github-portfolio-builder-india-kw-0172) covers the local hiring context, and [LinkedIn headline examples for freshers](/blog/linkedin-headline-examples-for-freshers-kw-0046) helps the people who find you on LinkedIn click through to your code.

faq.q: How many projects should a junior developer have on GitHub?
faq.a: Three to six pinned repositories is plenty. Two or three substantial, well-documented projects beat twenty half-finished ones. Unpin tutorials, course assignments and forks you have not meaningfully changed.

faq.q: Does the GitHub contribution graph matter to recruiters?
faq.a: A little, as a rough signal of consistency, but reviewers care far more about the quality of the repositories they open. Do not create fake activity; it is easy to spot and adds nothing.

faq.q: Should I make my college assignments public?
faq.a: Only if they are original, substantial and allowed by your institution's academic integrity policy. Most assignments look identical to thousands of others, so they rarely help a portfolio.

faq.q: Do I need a live demo for every project?
faq.a: Not every one, but your top project should have one if it has a user interface or API. If hosting is not possible, add a short screen recording or GIF and clear screenshots to the README.

faq.q: Is open-source contribution better than personal projects?
faq.a: They show different things. Personal projects show you can design and finish something; open-source pull requests show you can read an unfamiliar codebase and work with reviewers. A mix of both is ideal.
